grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Awakening from the Matrix: The Map
palavras: like waking up from the matrix
awakening from the matrix the map
resposta: Waking up from the Matrix is realizing the programs running in your mind that you didn't choose. Expanding consciousness is gaining space to choose. This path brings together three sources, each with its own stamp: the research of psychology and neuroscience, the wisdom of tradition, and what no one yet knows. Say wake-up lessons to see the full list.
aprofundar: The map has four gates. First, look at the program: conditioning, advertising, repetition and biases, all studied in the lab. Second, to see who sees: the attention, the observer self and the reality-predicting brain. Third, training: meditation, lucid dreaming, state of flow and neuroplasticity. Fourth, don't get lost along the way: separate tradition from fact and recognize spiritual deviance. Practice: pick a gate and say its name, for example cognitive biases or observer me.
camada3: For contemplation: Plato wrote that the liberated, when he leaves the cave, first becomes obscured and wants to return. Awakening doesn't start with light, it starts with discomfort. What uncomfortable truth have you been avoiding to look at?
seguir: Cognitive bias: the code of the Matrix.
Getting out of the Matrix in practice

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Consciousness Expansion: What Science Measures
resposta: Science doesn't measure the expansion of consciousness the way mystics talk about it, but it measures states of consciousness. In 1969, psychologist Charles Tart published Altered States of Consciousness, and today sleep, dreaming, meditation, hypnosis, and the effect of substances are studied with electroencephalogram and MRI.
aprofundar: In 2013, Italian and American researchers created a brain complexity index that accurately separates people who are awake, asleep, anesthetized, or in a coma. In 2017, a study showed that psychedelics increase the diversity of brain signals above normal wakefulness. It doesn't prove that the person has become wiser; it shows that the brain has become more variable, and what that means is still a hypothesis. Expansion, in the sense of more lucidity, compassion and clarity, is seen in life, not just in examination. Practice: After any strong experience, ask yourself: Am I gentler and more lucid, or just more impressed?
camada3: For contemplation: William James, in The Varieties of Religious Experience, 1902, judged spiritual experiences by their fruits, not their intensity. His question remains: What did that experience do to his life?
seguir: Default mode network: the inner chatterbox

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: The digital cave
resposta: In Plato's cave, prisoners saw shadows projected by others and thought they were reality. Today, the wall is the screen, and the shadow picker is an algorithm. In 2011, activist Eli Pariser called this a filter bubble: each person is given a custom-made world to capture their attention.
aprofundar: The whole truth: studies published in 2023 in the journals Science and Nature, using data from Facebook and Instagram, showed that the separation exists, but that changing the algorithm for a few months hardly changed people's political views. The strongest bubble isn't just the algorithm bubble: it's the one we choose ourselves, following only those who agree with us. Practice: Follow three serious sources today who think differently from you, and read without answering.
camada3: To contemplate: in Plato's cave there were chains. In the digital cave, the door is open, and yet we stay. What keeps you on the screen when nothing forces you?

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: The Trilemma of Simulation
palavras: how do we know if we re living in a simulation
como saber se vivemos numa simulacao
resposta: Nick Bostrom's 2003 argument does not say that we live in a simulation. It says that at least one of three things is true: almost all civilizations go extinct before they can simulate worlds; or those that do don't; or we almost certainly live in a simulation. No one knows which of the three is the real one.
aprofundar: In 2012, physicists Silas Beane, Zohreh Davoudi and Martin Savage proposed looking for signs of a simulation grid in very high-energy cosmic rays; nothing has been found to date. Critics, such as physicist Sabine Hossenfelder, say that without a possible test, the idea is closer to philosophy than science. Bostrom himself does not claim that we live in a simulation. Practice: separate three lists: what I know, what I assume, and what I wish were true.
camada3: To contemplate: the question is old. In India, Maya; in China, the butterfly of Zhuangzi; in the West, the evil genius of Descartes. Simulation or not, the pain of whoever's next to you is real to him. How would you live if that was enough?

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: The Brain as a Filter for Reality
palavras: the brain as a filter for reality
resposta: You don't see the world directly: your brain assembles an image of it. That's been proven. Each eye has a blind spot, no light receptor, and you can't see the hole because your brain fills it. In 2015, a photo of a dress divided the world into blue and black and white and gold: the same image, different brains.
aprofundar: The strongest hypothesis today, called predictive processing, says that the brain works the opposite of what we think: it predicts what you're going to perceive and uses your senses to correct the guess. Hermann von Helmholtz already spoke of unconscious inference in the 19th century. Neuroscientist Anil Seth, in his 2021 book Being You, sums it up: perception is a reality-controlled hallucination. It's a strong theory, but it's still being debated. Practice: Today, when you're absolutely sure of something you saw or heard, remember: my brain kicks too.
camada3: To contemplate: the sages of India called Maya the veil of perception. Neuroscience doesn't say the world is an illusion; it says your version of it is a construct. What part of your world is the world, and what part is your forecast about it?
seguir: Cognitive bias: the code of the Matrix.

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Default mode network: the inner chatterbox
palavras: default mode network the inner chatterbox
resposta: In 2001, neuroscientist Marcus Raichle described a brain network that becomes most active when you're not focused on anything: the default mode network. It's connected to thinking about yourself, ruminating on the past and imagining the future. It's largely the voice that talks nonstop inside your head.
aprofundar: In 2010, a Harvard study of more than 2,000 people showed that the mind wanders for almost half of the time you're awake, and that a wandering mind is a less happy mind. In 2011, Judson Brewer showed that experienced meditators have less activity in this network when meditating, and in 2012, Robin Carhart-Harris saw something similar to psilocybin. Careful, that doesn't make psychedelics a shortcut to enlightenment. In Brazil, psilocybin is banned outside of research, the religious use of ayahuasca is regulated, and there are real risks, like panic attacks and outbreaks in predisposed people. Practice: five minutes sitting, counting the number of times your mind goes out, and coming back without fighting.
camada3: To contemplate: the mystics called ego what neuroscience now sees, in part, as a network that can calm itself. It is not necessary to destroy the chatterer; it is enough to stop believing everything he says.

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: The Truth Made by Repetition
palavras: a lie repeated a thousand times
resposta: In 1977, psychologists Lynn Hasher, David Goldstein and Thomas Toppino showed that a repeated sentence seems more true even when it is false. It's the effect of illusory truth: the brain confuses what's familiar with what's real.
aprofundar: In 2015, psychologist Lisa Fazio showed that not even knowing the right answer completely protects: repetition deceives even those who know. That's why slogans, jingles, pulpit sticks and message boards work. Honest curiosity: the phrase a lie repeated a thousand times becomes truth is always attributed to Goebbels, but no one has found this phrase in his writings. The quote itself is an example of the effect. Practice: When an idea seems obvious, ask yourself: Have I checked it, or have I only heard it many times?
camada3: To contemplate: What you repeat to yourself every day also becomes true within you. What phrase about yourself did you repeat so much that you never questioned it again?

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Cognitive bias: the code of the Matrix.
palavras: cognitive bias the code of the matrix
resposta: If the Matrix had a source code, it would be cognitive biases, automatic shortcuts from the mind. In 1974, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described several of them, and Kahneman won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002. In his 2011 book Fast and Slow, he separates System 1, fast and automatic, from System 2, slow and reflexive.
aprofundar: Examples. Anchoring: In one experiment, a roulette wheel that stopped at 10 or 65 changed people's guess about the percentage of African countries in the UN. Availability: We find more common what we remember easily, like a plane crash seen on TV. Confirmation: We only look for what confirms what we already believe. No one gets rid of biases; you can recognize them and slow them down. Practice: Before making an important decision, get a good night's sleep and write down the best argument from the other side.
camada3: To contemplate: The most dangerous bias is to think that only others have biases. Psychologists call this the blind spot of bias. Where are you too sure?

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Attention: the power of the observer
palavras: attention the power of the observer
resposta: In 1999, psychologists Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris asked volunteers to count ball passes in a video. About half didn't see a person in a gorilla costume walk through the scene. It's inattentional blindness: what you don't respond to, to you, doesn't exist.
aprofundar: The psychologist William James wrote, in 1890, "My experience is what I agree to pay attention to". So attention is the most contested resource in the world: whoever controls your attention controls the reality you live in. Contemplative traditions have taught this for millennia. The observer of quantum physics is something else: it's physical measurement, not the human mind. Practice: For ten minutes today, give your full attention to a simple task, such as washing the dishes, and notice what you had not noticed.
camada3: To contemplate: the gorilla was always on the video. What gorilla could be going through your life right now while you're counting your passes?

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: States of consciousness: Gurdjieff and Wilber
palavras: states of consciousness gurdjieff and wilber
resposta: For George Gurdjieff, a master born in Armenia in the late nineteenth century, the average human being lives sleeping with his eyes open. According to the account of the disciple Piotr Ouspensky, in the book Fragments of an Unknown Teaching, he spoke of four states: sleep, ordinary wakefulness, which he called waking sleep, self-consciousness, and objective consciousness.
aprofundar: The path, for him, was self-remembering: being present to oneself while acting. In the late 20th century, philosopher Ken Wilber put together the integral theory, a map that links stages of developmental psychology with states described by contemplative traditions. They're maps of tradition and philosophy, useful for reflection, but no one's proven that consciousness goes up those stairs. Practice: set three alarms today; when you ring, ask: where am I, what am I feeling, and who is noticing this?
camada3: For contemplation: Gurdjieff taught that the first step is to realize that you are asleep, and that almost no one takes that step, because they are already awake. How many minutes today were you really present?

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: The Hawkins consciousness scale.
resposta: Psychiatrist David Hawkins, in his 1995 book Power versus Strength, created a scale of consciousness from one to a thousand: from shame, to twenty, to courage, to two hundred, and love, to five hundred, to enlightenment, to seven hundred to a thousand. The numbers were obtained by muscle testing, so-called applied kinesiology, and that's where the problem lies.
aprofundar: In controlled trials, in which neither the tester nor the test subject knows the correct answer, the muscle test did not fare better than chance, as in a 1988 study published in the Journal of the American Dietetic Association. So Hawkins' calibrations of people, books and countries have no measurable value. As a reflection map, the idea that courage comes before love can inspire; as a science, it doesn't hold up. Practice: When someone tells you that you measured the frequency of something, ask: with what device, and in a blind test?
camada3: To contemplate: no one needs a number to know if they acted out of fear or love. The most honest measure of consciousness is what you do when no one's looking.
seguir: States of consciousness: Gurdjieff and Wilber

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: The observing self
resposta: There's something in you that understands thoughts without being any of them. The Indian tradition of Vedanta calls it sakshi, the witness. Modern psychology uses the same idea: acceptance and commitment therapy, by Steven Hayes, talks about the self as context, and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy talks about decentralization.
aprofundar: Decentralization is seeing a thought as an event in the mind, not as a fact about the world. Clinical research shows that such therapy reduces relapses in those who have had multiple bouts of depression. Ramana Maharshi, the 20th-century Indian sage, taught one question: Who am I? Not to answer with words, but to direct attention to the questioner. Practice: When a heavy thought comes, put it in front: I'm having that thought, and repeat the whole sentence. Look at the space that opens up.
camada3: To contemplate: the sky is not the clouds. The clouds pass, the sky stays. Are you the time that changes, or the sky where it happens?

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Lucid dreaming: training to wake up
palavras: a lucid dream and waking up
lucid dreaming training to wake up
resposta: In 2021, teams from four countries, the United States, France, Germany and the Netherlands, talked to people during lucid dreaming: they asked simple questions and calculations, and the dreamers answered with eye movements, without waking up. The study appeared in the journal Current Biology. Waking up inside the dream is real and can be trained.
aprofundar: The most widely studied technique is Stephen LaBerge's MILD: when you wake up in the morning, you repeat the intention, the next time you dream, I'll realize I'm dreaming, and imagine the dream coming back to you lucid. In 2017, an Australian study by Denholm Aspy combined this with reality tests and waking up in the middle of the night; among those who went back to sleep quickly, almost half of the attempts were successful. Practice: Leave a notebook by your bed and write down your dreams when you wake up; remembering your dreams is the first step.
camada3: To contemplate: Tibetan dream yoga masters said that one who does not recognize the dream at night hardly recognizes the illusion of the day. Right now, how do you know you're awake?

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: State of flow
resposta: Psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi has studied for decades the moments when people feel most alive. In 1990, in his book Flow, he described the state of flow: total attention, time seems to disappear, the voice being criticized becomes silent, and the action flows almost by itself.
aprofundar: Flow comes when the challenge is slightly greater than the skill, with clear goals and immediate feedback. Too much challenge creates anxiety; too little, boredom. Athletes, musicians, craftsmen and surgeons describe the same state. It's one of the healthiest doors to egoless consciousness, because it's born of presence, not flight. Practice: Choose an activity you enjoy, turn off your cell phone for 90 minutes, and increase the difficulty a little.
camada3: To contemplate: in the flow you don't think of yourself, and yet you've never been so whole. Maybe freedom isn't having more of me, it's needing less of him.

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Mindfulness: What the Evidence Shows
resposta: In 1979, Jon Kabat-Zinn created at the University of Massachusetts an eight-week stress reduction program based on mindfulness. In 2014, a major review in JAMA Internal Medicine of 47 studies found moderate evidence of improvement in anxiety, depression, and pain.
aprofundar: The whole truth includes boundaries. The same review did not find meditation superior to other active treatments, such as exercise or therapy. In 2018, a group of researchers published the article Mind the Hype, warning of hype in the media. And in 2017, a study by Jared Lindahl and Willoughby Britton documented difficult experiences in meditators, such as fear and feelings of unreality. Meditation is powerful; it is neither miraculous nor risk-free. Practice: three minutes, three times a day: breathe and quietly name what you feel, without trying to change it.
camada3: To contemplate: Kabat-Zinn defines mindfulness as paying attention, purposefully, in the present moment, without judgment. The hardest part is almost always the last one. What did you judge today before you even looked?
seguir: Default mode network: the inner chatterbox

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Kundalini and chakras
resposta: Kundalini, in the tradition of tantra and hatha yoga, is an energy described as a sleeping snake at the base of the spine, rising through the chakras, subtle centers, to the top of the head. It's a teaching of tradition, centuries of practice, not a fact of anatomy.
aprofundar: Facts: The seven-chakra system known in the West comes mostly from a 1577 Indian text translated in 1919 by John Woodroffe in The Power of the Serpent. Older texts give different numbers of chakras, and the colors of the rainbow are a 20th-century Western creation. No tests found chakras on the body. Serious teachers warn that intense energy practices without guidance can lead to crises. Practice: Use your chakras as a map of attention: breathe by feeling the base of your spine, heart and top of your head, without expecting phenomena.
camada3: To contemplate: in the traditions, the snake does not ascend by force, but when the practitioner purifies himself and calms down. What about you needs calm before any power?

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Everything is Mind and Neuroscience
palavras: the whole and mind and science
o todo e mente e a ciencia
resposta: The Caibalion, 1908, teaches that the Whole is Mind. Neuroscience shows something more modest but real: your mind depends on your brain, because anesthesia, deep sleep, and injury change or erase your consciousness. At the same time, no one has yet explained why feeling exists. Both things are true at the same time.
aprofundar: In philosophy, the idea that reality is mental is called idealism. Bishop George Berkeley wrote in 1710 that to be is to be perceived. Today, some thinkers, such as Bernardo Kastrup, advocate modern idealism, others panpsychism, and most neuroscientists work with the hypothesis that consciousness arises from the brain. None of this is proven. What's proven to be more practical is that the way you interpret a fact changes your emotion, and that's the basis of Aaron Beck's cognitive therapy. Practice: When you feel a strong emotion, write down the fact and, next to it, the interpretation you gave to it.
camada3: To contemplate: the hermetist says that everything is mind; the scientist says that mind comes from the brain; the mystic says that he who asks is already the mystery itself. All three agree on one point: Your mind is where you live. How's that house?

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Signs of Spiritual Awakening and Departure
palavras: signs of spiritual awakening and departure
resposta: Signs of a true awakening, according to tradition: less reactivity, more honesty with yourself, more compassion and less need to be right. On the other hand, lists of ascension symptoms, such as ringing in the ear, headache, or tiredness as evidence of awakening, are myths: These symptoms have causes in the body and merit medical examination.
aprofundar: In 1984, psychotherapist John Welwood coined the term spiritual deviance: using spirituality to escape from wounds, anger, grief, or practical problems. Examples: saying that everything is an illusion to avoid facing a conflict, or having someone vibrate loudly to silence a pain. There are also real crises along the way: St. John of the Cross, in the sixteenth century, spoke of the dark night of the soul, and Stanislav and Christina Grof, in 1989, of spiritual emergency. Since 1994, the American Psychiatric Manual has recognized the religious or spiritual problem as worthy of attention, without calling it madness. Practice: If a spiritual experience robs you of sleep, work, or peace for days, seek professional help; it does not erase your path.
camada3: To contemplate: the awakening fleeing pain is still asleep. What pain did you call illusion so you didn't have to feel it?

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Getting out of the Matrix in practice
palavras: get out of the matrix in practice
how to check a news story
getting out of the matrix in practice
resposta: Three steps with evidence. One, media diet: In an experiment published in 2020 in American Economic Review, people who turned off Facebook for four weeks spent more time with family and friends, became a little less polarized, and reported more well-being. Two, critical thinking. Three, silence.
aprofundar: Critical thinking in practice: Stanford researchers, with Sam Wineburg, found that professional reviewers don't read a website from top to bottom; they open other tabs and look up who's behind it. This is called lateral reading. Mike Caulfield's SIFT method is summarized in four steps: stop, investigate the source, find better coverage, and trace the claim back to the source. And silence: a time a day without any stimulus, to listen to what's yours. Practice: for a week, news only once a day, at set times, and no screens first thing in the morning.
camada3: To contemplate: Leaving the Matrix is not isolating yourself from the world or distrusting everything, it's just another prison. It's choosing what goes into your mind. If your mind was a house, who has the key to it today?
seguir: How to Get Out of the Matrix

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Neuroplasticity: the brain reprograms itself
resposta: The adult brain changes with use. In 2000, neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire showed that taxi drivers in London, who line thousands of streets, have the back of the hippocampus, which is connected to spatial memory, larger than other people. In 2004, another study saw changes in the brains of people who learned to juggle in three months.
aprofundar: Psychologist Donald Hebb proposed in 1949 the rule that neuroscientist Carla Shatz summarized as follows: neurons firing together connect. Every repeated habit strengthens a path, and every abandoned path weakens it. Honesty: the word has become marketing. No ten-minute audio reprograms the brain, and the twenty-one-day story is a myth: In 2010, a study by Phillippa Lally found an average of sixty-six days for a habit to become automatic. Practice: Pick a small habit, always on the same schedule, and count two months, not three weeks.
camada3: To contemplate: conditioning and release use the same tool, repetition. The difference is who chooses what repeats. What have you been repeating without choosing?

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Hebb's rule: neurons firing together.
palavras: hebb s rule neurons firing together
resposta: In 1949, Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb proposed in his book The Organization of Behavior that when one neuron repeatedly helps to fire another, the bond between the two is strengthened. The popular phrase, neurons firing together connect, is a summary made later. Today, this idea is one of the cornerstones of memory science.
aprofundar: The proof came in 1973: Timothy Bliss and Terje Lømo stimulated the hippocampus of rabbits with electrical bursts and saw the synapses respond more strongly for hours, sometimes days. They called it long-lasting enhancement. Eric Kandel, studying the sea slug Aplysia, showed that short memories change the strength of synapses, and that long memories require new proteins and even new connections; he won the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2000. Honesty: Hebb's rule explains part of learning, not all of it. The brain also weakens and cuts connections, and that's just as important as strengthening. Practice: To learn something, put together at the same time what you want to connect, a new word, an image, and a phrase of your own, and repeat on different days, not all at once.
camada3: To contemplate: every thought you repeat is a trail you yourself open in the woods. What trail have you been treading so far that it already looks like a road?
seguir: Habits: the autopilot of the base ganglia
Sleep: When the brain records the day

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Taxi Drivers and Musicians - The Brain That Trains
palavras: taxi drivers and musicians - the brain that trains
resposta: To get their licence, London taxi drivers spend three to four years memorizing about 25,000 streets. In 2011, Katherine Woollett and Eleanor Maguire followed seventy-nine learners: those who passed the test gained volume in the back of the hippocampus; those who did not and the comparison group did not. It was proof that training changes the brain, and not just that different brains choose careers.
aprofundar: But there's a price. In 2006, Maguire's team compared taxi drivers to bus drivers, who drive all day on fixed routes: Taxi drivers had the back of the hippocampus larger and the front smaller, and did worse at memorizing a new figure. The brain reallocates space, it doesn't grow for free. In musicians: In 1995, Thomas Elbert and colleagues showed that violinists and cellists have a larger area in the cortex for the fingers of the left hand, the one that grips the strings, and the effect was greater in those who started early. In the same year, Alvaro Pascual-Leone saw the map of the fingers grow in five days of piano practice, and change also in who he just imagined playing. Caution: many studies of musicians compare groups that were already different, and the samples are small; the size of these effects, and especially the power of the imagined training, is still a hypothesis. Practice: Practice something difficult in short, daily sessions, and at the end of the day, practice with your eyes closed for two minutes.
camada3: To contemplate: each person's brain is a map of the life they've lived. If someone could read yours, what would you say you practiced the most?
seguir: Critical periods - the windows of childhood

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Does meditation change the brain? What Is Really Known
palavras: does meditation change the brain what is really known
resposta: That meditation changes brain activity during practice is well established. Whether it changes the structure of the brain is still up for debate. In 2005, Harvard's Sara Lazar found thicker cortex in areas of attention and body perception in 20 experienced meditators compared to 15 non-meditators.
aprofundar: In 2004, Antoine Lutz and Richard Davidson recorded very strong gamma waves in Tibetan monks with tens of thousands of hours of practice, but there were only eight monks. In 2011, Britta Hölzel reported more gray matter in the hippocampus after eight weeks of the stress reduction program with sixteen people. Now the honest part: In 2022, Davidson's own team published two trials together, with two hundred and eighteen randomized subjects, and found no change in brain structure after eight weeks. Small samples tend to exaggerate effects, and larger studies tend to shrink them. What stands out: meditation trains attention and helps with stress, as reviews show; the promise of a new brain in eight weeks has not been confirmed. Practice: Meditate on what changes in your life, not on a brain scan.
camada3: To reflect: teachers never measured practice by the size of the brain, but by the quality of presence. If no test showed a difference, would you still meditate?
seguir: Default mode network: the inner chatterbox

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Adult neurogenesis: are new neurons born?
palavras: adult neurogenesis are new neurons born
resposta: For almost a century, it has been taught that the adult brain does not gain new neurons. In mice and rats, it's now proven to win in the hippocampus. In adult humans, the question remains open, and serious laboratories have come up with conflicting answers.
aprofundar: In 1998, Peter Eriksson and Fred Gage found new neurons in the hippocampus of cancer patients who had received a cell division marker. In 2013, Jonas Frisén's team used the carbon-14 scattered in the air by nuclear tests and estimated about 700 new neurons a day in each hippocampus. In 2018, the journal Nature published Shawn Sorrells' study, which found virtually no new neurons after childhood; in the same year, Maura Boldrini found the opposite, and in 2019 María Llorens-Martín's team found thousands of young neurons in people up to eighty-seven years old. Part of the difference could be in how the tissue was preserved. Hence the seal: in humans, as yet unknown, with a promising hypothesis. Be careful who sells a supplement that makes neurons grow: it hasn't been proven. Practice: What helps the brain does not depend on this response: sleep, movement and learning new things.
camada3: To contemplate: even science sometimes wakes up from an old certainty. What dogma about yourself, like I'm like this and I don't change, deserves the same re-examination?
seguir: Stress and Exercise: What Shrinks and What Feeds the Hippocampus
Sleep: When the brain records the day

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Brain maps: Merzenich, Taub and the aftermath of a stroke
palavras: brain maps merzenich, taub and the aftermath of a stroke
resposta: In the 1980s, Michael Merzenich showed in monkeys that the map of the body inside the brain changes: when one finger stopped sending signals, its area was used by the neighboring fingers. Psychologist Edward Taub turned this idea into a treatment for stroke patients: limiting the good arm to force the weak arm to work.
aprofundar: Taub called the problem not-learned use: After a stroke, the person gives up the weak arm, and the brain shrinks its space even further. In induced restraint therapy, the healthy arm stays in a glove for a good portion of the day, and the weak arm trains for several hours a day for two weeks. In 2006, the EXCITE trial of 222 patients, published in the journal JAMA, showed greater improvement than standard treatment, and it lasted at least a year. Honestly, therapy is for people who still have some movement, and most recovery happens in the first few months. Taub's monkey experiments led to a 1981 animal abuse lawsuit; he was convicted, but the conviction was overturned in 1983 because the state law did not apply to federally funded laboratories. Beware, too, of games that promise to turn your brain: In 2016, the Lumosity company struck a two-million-dollar deal with the U.S. government for unproven advertising. Practice: If someone in your family has had a stroke, seek rehabilitation from the NHS or a physical therapist as soon as possible; time is of the essence.
camada3: To contemplate: what you don't use, the brain lends to something else. What ability of yours is stored in your fear-trapped arm, waiting to be used again?
seguir: Taxi Drivers and Musicians - The Brain That Trains
Critical periods - the windows of childhood

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Critical periods - the windows of childhood
palavras: critical periods - the windows of childhood
resposta: Some brain capacities have windows in which they form much more easily. In the 1960s, David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel closed the eye of a kitten for a few months, and that eye lost much of its connection to the brain. In adult cats, the same thing didn't happen. They won the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1981.
aprofundar: In children, it's the logic of amblyopia, the lazy eye: treated early, with a tampon or glasses, usually has good results; treated late, the gain is usually less. With language too: those who learn a language after adolescence rarely lose their accent. In 2018, a study of about six hundred and seventy thousand people estimated that the ease of mastering the grammar of a new language drops around the age of seventeen. The hopeful part: Closed window is not locked door. Adults continue to learn languages, music and crafts, only with more effort, and there is research, still in the field of hypothesis, that tries to reopen windows in adults. Practice: If you are caring for a child, take him to the eye doctor in the first few years of life; and if you are an adult, change the older one because it will require more training.
camada3: For contemplation: many Matrix programs enter through the open window of childhood before we can choose. What belief of yours has come through that window and not yet been reviewed with adult eyes?
seguir: Reprogramming beliefs in practice: reassessment and cognitive therapy

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Sleep: When the brain records the day
palavras: sleep when the brain records the day
resposta: Sleep is not shutting down: it's when the brain organizes what it's learned. In 1924, John Jenkins and Karl Dallenbach showed that people forgot less of a list of syllables when they slept after studying than when they woke up. Today, that sleep helps fix memories is one of science's most repeated findings.
aprofundar: In 1994, Matthew Wilson and Bruce McNaughton saw, in mice, hippocampal neurons repeating during sleep the sequence of paths taken in the maze, much like a daydreamer. In 2002, Matthew Walker showed that people who trained a sequence of fingers on the keyboard got faster after a night's sleep, without further training. The idea that sleep washes the brain, through the so-called glymphatic system, came from studies on mice in 2013 and is still a hypothesis in humans. Honesty: Walker's own book Why We Sleep has been criticized for exaggerating some numbers. Sleep is very important, and it doesn't need to be exaggerated. Practice: Study or practice something at the end of the day, sleep seven to nine hours, and review the next day before learning something new.
camada3: To contemplate: traditions call sleep a small death and awakening a daily rebirth. What do you deliver at night, and what do you choose to take with you into the new day?

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Habits: the autopilot of the base ganglia
palavras: habits the autopilot of the base ganglia
resposta: When an action becomes a habit, the command passes from the front areas of the brain, which decide, to the basal ganglia, a set of nuclei at the back of it. Neuroscientist Ann Graybiel at MIT has seen in mice that with repetition, the neurons in the striatum start firing loudly at the beginning and end of the routine, as if they were packing everything into one block.
aprofundar: So habit dispenses with decision: one trigger fires the whole pack. In 2002, Wendy Wood and colleagues asked people to write down what they did throughout the day: About 43 percent of the actions were repeated almost every day in the same place, often while the person was thinking about something else. Two lessons have good evidence. First, habits depend on the environment; changing your home, your route, or your schedule weakens the trigger, and it's a good time to change habits. Second, plans like if such a thing happens, then I do such another, called implementation intentions, increased the chances of meeting goals in a review of 94 studies, published in 2006 by Peter Gollwitzer and Paschal Sheeran. Practice: write a sentence today like this: When I sit on the couch at night, I'm going to leave my phone in the kitchen.
camada3: To contemplate: the ganglia of the base do not judge; they guard with equal care the habit that liberates and that which imprisons. Who's picking the triggers for your day?

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: The placebo effect: the real power of expectation
palavras: the placebo effect the real power of expectation
resposta: The placebo is real, but it's not magic. In 1978, Jon Levine and colleagues gave fake medicine to patients with tooth extraction pain; many felt relief, and that relief was lessened with naloxone, which blocks the body's natural morphine. The anticipation made the brain release its own painkillers.
aprofundar: In 2001, a study in the journal Science showed that Parkinson's patients released dopamine into the brain when they thought they had been given the drug. In 2010, Ted Kaptchuk of Harvard gave a placebo to 80 people with irritable bowel syndrome, openly telling them it was a placebo, and even so their symptoms improved more than in the group that got nothing; how this works is still a hypothesis. Now the limits: a 2010 Cochrane review of more than 200 trials found placebo effect mostly on what you feel, like pain and nausea, and little or nothing on what you measure in your body. Placebo doesn't shrink a tumor or cure an infection. And there's the opposite: nocebo, when fear of side effects produces real symptoms. Practice: Expectation is not a substitute for treatment, but can be added to it; follow the indicated treatment and also take care of the trust and care around you.
camada3: To contemplate: the placebo shows that belief has a body. That is why it matters so much who plants your beliefs, and with what interest. Who profits when you believe?
seguir: Reprogramming beliefs in practice: reassessment and cognitive therapy

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Stress and Exercise: What Shrinks and What Feeds the Hippocampus
palavras: stress and exercise what shrinks and what feeds the hippocampus
resposta: Endless stress and regular movement pull the hippocampus, the center of memory, in opposite directions. In 2011, Kirk Erickson and colleagues randomly assigned 120 older adults: those who walked three times a week for a year had a hippocampus about two percent larger; in the group that only did stretching, it shrank a little, as is common with age.
aprofundar: In the same study, the increase was accompanied by BDNF, a protein that functions as a fertilizer for neurons; in 1999, Henriette van Praag had already seen that mice that ran on the wheel produced more new neurons. On the other hand, cortisol, the stress hormone, in excess and for a long time damages neurons in the hippocampus in animals, as Robert Sapolsky's work has shown; and people with Cushing's syndrome, who produce too much cortisol, have the smaller hippocampus, which partially regrows after treatment. Honesty: In 2002, a study of twins showed that the smaller hippocampus of post-traumatic stress veterans also appeared in the twin who never went to war. So part of it could be a pre-existing vulnerability, not just stress damage. And BDNF measured in the blood is not the same as in the brain. Practice: Thirty to forty minutes of walking at a pace that leaves you a little gasping, three times a week, and a break to breathe slowly when stress strikes.
camada3: To contemplate: many masters have taught on foot, from Aristotle to monks who meditate on foot. What thought of yours will only resolve when you put your body into motion?
seguir: Adult neurogenesis: are new neurons born?
Sleep: When the brain records the day

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Reprogramming beliefs in practice: reassessment and cognitive therapy
palavras: reprogramming beliefs in practice reassessment and cognitive therapy
resposta: Beliefs cannot be changed by decree, but they can be tested and reviewed. In the '60s, psychiatrist Aaron Beck realized that depressed patients had automatic thoughts, like I always fail, that they accepted without examining. This was the birth of cognitive behavioral therapy, now one of the most studied psychotherapies in the world.
aprofundar: The central technique is called cognitive reassessment: note the thought, look for the evidence for and against it, and assemble a fairer reading. Imaging studies, like those by Kevin Ochsner and James Gross, show that reevaluating a situation activates areas of the front of the brain and decreases the amygdala response, which is linked to fear. In 2012, Stefan Hofmann gathered two hundred and sixty-nine meta-analyses and found good support for this therapy in anxiety, depression and other problems. Honestly, it's not the only one that works, other serious therapies have had similar results, and a 2015 review suggested that its effect on depression has diminished over the years. And changing a deeply held belief takes weeks of practice, not a phrase repeated in the mirror. Practice: Today, when you feel a strong emotion, write three lines: what happened, what I thought, and what other explanation would also be possible. If the distress is great, look for a board-certified psychologist.
camada3: To reflect: the Stoic philosopher Epictetus once said that it is not the things that disturb us, but the judgment we make of them, and Beck himself recognized this root. What judgment of yours today deserves a second trial?

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Myth: Left brain and right brain
palavras: myth left brain and right brain
resposta: Myth: There are no left-brained, logical people and right-brained, creative people. In 2013, researchers at the University of Utah analyzed scans of more than 1,000 people and found no one who used one whole side of the brain more than the other.
aprofundar: The real seed of the myth: some functions hang to one side. In the vast majority of right-handed people, language is more on the left side, as Paul Broca and Carl Wernicke pointed out in the 19th century. And Roger Sperry, studying people who had the connection between the two halves cut off to treat severe epilepsy, showed that each half processes things in a different way; he won the Nobel Prize in 1981. That's been proven. But in a healthy brain, the two halves work together all the time: math, creativity and music use both halves. The myth became a personality test and a groundless training course. The other popular myth, that we only use 10 percent of the brain, has its own lesson: say 10 percent of the brain. Practice: Be suspicious of any test that tells you what kind of brain you have.
camada3: To contemplate: labels like I'm not creative or I'm not numbers are more arresting than any anatomy. What label have you accepted on your own brain?
seguir: We only use 10% of the brain
Cognitive bias: the code of the Matrix.

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Reprogram DNA with your mind? Epigenetics without exaggeration
palavras: reprogram dna with your mind epigenetics without exaggeration
resposta: Myth: Thoughts don't rewrite the letters of your DNA, and there are no dormant strands of DNA to activate. What's real has another name, epigenetics: chemical markers that turn genes on and off, and that change with diet, stress, smoking and age.
aprofundar: The most famous example comes from the Dutch famine winter of 1944 and 1945: a 2008 study showed that six decades later, people who were in the womb during the famine had different markings on a gene linked to growth. That's been proven. And studies of meditation and genes, like one from 2014 in which 19 experienced meditators showed a decrease in inflammation gene activity after a day of practice, are small and preliminary: hypothesis. Books like The Biology of Belief, by Bruce Lipton, take this true science and stretch it into promises it doesn't hold. And twelve-string DNA, or DNA activation by frequencies and paid courses, has no basis whatsoever. Practice: When someone sells DNA reprogramming, ask: What gene, what measurement, what study, and with how many people?
camada3: For contemplation: you don't rewrite your code, but you choose every day the environment in which it expresses itself: what it eats, how it sleeps, who it lives with. What environment are you giving your genes?
seguir: Stress and Exercise: What Shrinks and What Feeds the Hippocampus
The placebo effect: the real power of expectation

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Metacognition and neuroplasticity: the mind and the brain
palavras: awareness of one s own thinking
metacognition and neuroplasticity the mind and the brain
resposta: Metacognition is thinking about your own thinking: realizing what you know, what you don't know, and how your mind is working right now. Neuroplasticity is another thing: it's the brain physically changing with use, in synapses and connections. One is a function of the mind; the other is a change in the organ. And the two of them work together.
aprofundar: Think of a ship. Neuroplasticity is the hull being slowly reshaped by the journey itself; metacognition is the captain looking at the map and correcting the course. On its own, plasticity reinforces anything that repeats itself, including fear and addiction. Metacognition helps you choose what's worth repeating. And the way back: observing one's thoughts, repeated every day, is also training, and training changes the brain. Honestly, nobody yet knows exactly what physical changes support better metacognition; there are clues in the front of the brain, which you'll see in the lesson on measuring metacognition. Practice: three times today, stop and ask yourself, what am I thinking right now, and how do I know this is true?
camada3: To contemplate: the brain shapes the mind, and the mind, through attention, shapes the brain. In that wheel, where does your freedom begin?
seguir: Flavell, Nelson and Narens: knowing, watching and controlling

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Flavell, Nelson and Narens: knowing, watching and controlling
palavras: flavell, nelson and narens knowing, watching and controlling
resposta: In 1979, the American psychologist John Flavell, who studied children, popularized the name metacognition and separated it into two parts: knowledge about how the mind works, for example knowing that you forget names, and regulation, which is using that knowledge to plan, check, and correct. In 1990, Thomas Nelson and Louis Narens described the mechanism: a monitoring level and a controlling level.
aprofundar: In Nelson and Narens' model, there are two floors. At the bottom, the mind works: it reads, remembers, solves. Upstairs, she watches herself. Monitoring is the information that comes up: that I already know, that is difficult, that word is on the tip of my tongue. Control is the descending order: study more, change strategy, stop trying. If monitoring is wrong, control is wrong too: those who think they already know stop studying too soon. Back in 1970, Flavell and colleagues had already seen that young children think they'll remember a lot more than they actually do, and that this illusion diminishes with age. Practice: Before a task, ask what you know about it; in the middle, ask if it's working; at the end, ask what you would do differently.
camada3: To contemplate: in you there are those who act and those who watch. What changes when the spectator also has the right to correct the route?
seguir: Calibration: certainty, accuracy and the Dunning-Kruger effect
Learning to learn: the illusion of fluency and recovery practice

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Calibration: certainty, accuracy and the Dunning-Kruger effect
palavras: he who knows little thinks he knows much
calibration certainty, accuracy and the dunning-kruger effect
quem sabe pouco acha que sabe muito
resposta: Calibration is how much your certainty matches your accuracy: whoever says ninety percent sure should get it right nine times out of ten. For most people, certainty is more important than success. In 1999, Justin Kruger and David Dunning showed that participants with the lowest scores on tests of logic, grammar and humor were, on average, in the 12th percentile, but placed themselves in the 62nd.
aprofundar: Kruger and Dunning explained it this way: the same skill that is lacking to do well is needed to realize that one has done wrong. Now the honest criticism: since 2016, Edward Nuhfer and colleagues, and then Gilles Gignac and Marcin Zajenkowski, have shown that much of the famous graph appears even with randomly drawn data, by a statistical effect called mean regression, coupled with the general tendency of everyone to find themselves above the average. Today the effect is debated: overconfidence is real and common; the idea that the less skilled are the more deluded may be far less than it seemed. On the bright side, calibration is practiced. In the Good Judgment Project prediction tournament, published in 2014, a short probability workout improved participants' calibration. Practice: Today, before you make an important statement, give a percentage of certainty and write it down; at the end of the month, check how accurate it is.
camada3: To contemplate: Socrates said he knew he knew nothing. Perhaps the wisdom is not to have fewer certainties, but certainties of the right size. What certainty of yours is too great?
seguir: Cognitive bias: the code of the Matrix.

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: The illusion of explanatory depth
resposta: Do you know how a zipper works? Almost everyone says yes, until I try to explain step by step. In 2002, Leonid Rozenblit and Frank Keil of Yale University asked people to rate how much they understood about common objects, such as zippers, drains, and locks; after they wrote down the explanation, the ratings they gave themselves plummeted.
aprofundar: The illusion is stronger for mechanisms, things with gears and causes, than for loose facts or stories. In 2013, Philip Fernbach and colleagues took this to politics: asking people to explain how a proposal would work, step by step, decreased certainty and made opinions less extreme; asking only for reasons for one's position did not have the same effect. Part of the illusion comes from something healthy: we live in a network of knowledge, and we confuse what the community knows with what's in our heads. Practice: When you have a strong opinion, try explaining out loud, step by step, how it works. Where you lock, there your search begins.
camada3: To contemplate: many quarrels are between two illusions of understanding. What would happen in their discussions if each side had to explain the mechanism first?
seguir: Calibration: certainty, accuracy and the Dunning-Kruger effect

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Measure metacognition: the meta-d line and the prefrontal cortex
palavras: measure metacognition the meta-d line and the prefrontal cortex
resposta: Metacognition can be measured. In simple tasks, the person answers and then says how much he or she trusts the answer. People with good metacognitive sensitivity trust more when they're right and less when they're wrong. In 2012, Brian Maniscalco and Hakwan Lau created a measure called the meta-d line, which separates this sensitivity from performance on the task itself.
aprofundar: In 2010, Stephen Fleming and colleagues in London showed in the journal Science that people with more precise introspection on a visual task had more gray matter in the anterior prefrontal cortex, the most forward part of the brain, which is highly developed in humans. In 2014, the same Fleming studied seven patients with lesions in this area: metacognition worsened in perceptual tasks, but not in memory tasks. The caveat: the samples are small, most are correlation and not cause, and metacognition seems to depend on the type of task; evaluating one's own vision well does not guarantee evaluating one's own memory well. The idea of a single metacognition center in the brain is hypothetical. Practice: In a question-and-answer game with friends, give each answer a confidence rating of one to five, and see if your fives are more accurate than your ones.
camada3: To contemplate: knowing that you don't know is a kind of knowing, and perhaps the rarest. In what area of your life are you good, but poorly calibrated about how good you are?
seguir: Calibration: certainty, accuracy and the Dunning-Kruger effect
Lucid dreaming and metacognition: the same light on?

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Learning to learn: the illusion of fluency and recovery practice
palavras: learning to learn the illusion of fluency and recovery practice
resposta: Re-reading and scribbling give the feeling of having learned, because the text is familiar. It's called the fluency illusion. In 2006, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke showed that students who tested themselves remembered much more after a week than those who only repeated, although those who repeated felt more confident.
aprofundar: The problem is metacognitive: we judge learning by the ease of the moment, and ease deceives. A 2013 review by John Dunlosky and colleagues evaluated ten study techniques: test practice and spaced study scored high; scribbling and rereading scored low. Another useful finding: judgments about whether you've learned are much more accurate when they're made a while later, rather than right after you've studied, as Thomas Nelson and John Dunlosky showed in 1991. The effort that seems to get in the way, the difficulty in remembering, is precisely what it engraves; psychologist Robert Bjork calls this desirable difficulty. Practice: Close the book and write down everything that comes to mind; then check it out. Repeat after a day, three days and a week.
camada3: To reflect: What seems easy is not always what it is, and what costs is not always a sign of failure. Where in your life have you confused familiarity with wisdom?
seguir: Sleep: When the brain records the day

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Metacognitive therapy: the beliefs behind worry
palavras: metacognitive therapy the beliefs behind worry
resposta: The British psychologist Adrian Wells proposed in the 1990s that the problem with anxiety and depression is not just what we think, but what we believe about thinking. Beliefs like worrying protects me, or I can't control my thoughts, keep my mind stuck in worry and rumination. He created metacognitive therapy to mess with those beliefs.
aprofundar: Wells calls this pattern cognitive-attentional syndrome: worrying, ruminating, watching for threats and trying to suppress thoughts. Positive beliefs say that worry helps; negative beliefs say that it is dangerous and uncontrollable. The two together form the trap. Instead of discussing the content of each fear, therapy teaches you to let go and postpone worrying for a set time. A 2018 meta-analysis by Nicoline Normann and Nexhmedin Morina, of twenty-five studies, found large effects, and even advantage over cognitive behavioral therapy. Honesty: The authors themselves ask for larger studies before firm conclusions, and many trials involve the creator and his collaborators, which can inflate results. Practice: when a concern comes up, tell it: not now; at eighteen o'clock I give you fifteen minutes. At the appointed time, many have already lost their strength. If your anxiety is severe, see a psychologist.
camada3: For contemplation: Many traditions teach not to feed thoughts, nor to fight with them. What concern of yours do you believe is protecting you, when in fact it only occupies the place of action?
seguir: Decentralization: Thought is an event, not a fact

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Decentralization: Thought is an event, not a fact
palavras: decentralization thought is an event, not a fact
resposta: Decentralization is taking a step back and seeing a thought as a mind event, and not as the truth about yourself or about the world. In 2002, John Teasdale and colleagues showed that this ability, which they called metacognitive awareness, grew with mindfulness-based cognitive therapy and was linked to fewer relapses of depression.
aprofundar: In the 2000 trial, Teasdale, Zindel Segal, and Mark Williams followed 145 people recovering from depression. Among those who had already had three or more seizures, the relapse dropped from sixty-six to thirty-seven percent with the program. In 2016, Willem Kuyken gathered the individual data of one thousand two hundred and fifty-eight patients from nine trials: the risk of relapse in just over a year was about thirty percent lower. The limitations: the benefit is clearer for people who've had multiple seizures, and in a large trial in 2015, the program was no better than continuing on the antidepressant; it was similar. No one should stop a medicine on their own. Practice: When a heavy thought comes up, name the category, for example, look at the failure story again, and turn your attention back to three breaths.
camada3: To contemplate: the sky is not the clouds, even when they cover everything. What cloud do you call heaven?
seguir: Cognitive effusion: letting go of the hook of words

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Cognitive effusion: letting go of the hook of words
palavras: cognitive effusion letting go of the hook of words
resposta: In acceptance and commitment therapy, created by Steven Hayes, fusion is when you and thought see one thing only: I'm a failure ceases to be a phrase and becomes reality. Diffusion is perceiving words as words, sounds and images in the mind, without obeying them and without fighting with them.
aprofundar: An old technique shows the effect: in 1916, psychologist Edward Titchener noticed that repeating a word too many times, like milk, milk, milk, causes it to lose meaning for a moment. In 2004, Akihiko Masuda and colleagues asked people to repeat out loud, quickly, a word linked to a negative thought about themselves; the discomfort and credibility of the thought dropped more than with distraction or with attempts to control the thought. A 2015 meta-analysis of thirty-nine trials found acceptance and commitment therapy to be better than waiting list and standard treatment, and similar to cognitive behavioral therapy. Honesty: Whether infusion is really the ingredient that makes therapy work is still a hypothesis, and the effect of repetition is transient. Practice: Take the sentence that weighs the most on you, summarize it in one word, and repeat out loud for 30 seconds. Then say, "Thank you, lie, for the story".
camada3: To contemplate: words are fingers pointing at the moon, says a Zen teaching. Have you confused a finger with the moon itself?
seguir: Decentralization: Thought is an event, not a fact

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: System 2 to the rescue? The limits of debiasing
palavras: system 2 to the rescue the limits of debiasing
resposta: Knowing that biases exist is not enough to escape them. In 2012, Richard West, Russell Meserve and Keith Stanovich showed that people with higher cognitive ability did not have a blind spot of minor bias: they continued to see biases in others more than in themselves, and sometimes even more.
aprofundar: Still, some training works a little. Consider the opposite technique, tested by Charles Lord, Mark Lepper and Elizabeth Preston in 1984, reduced confirmation bias better than just asking people to be impartial. In 2019, Anne-Laure Sellier, Irene Scopelliti, and Carey Morewedge gave a training set against confirmation bias to two hundred and ninety graduate students; then, in a business case without any warning, inspired by the decision to launch the space shuttle Challenger, the trained chose nineteen percent less of the biased solution. It's good news, but limited: the gains are worth more to the trained bias and similar situations; a general training that leaves the person rational in everything has no support. It usually works best to change the environment: checklist, second opinion, and time to decide. Practice: Before making a decision, write down three reasons why you might be wrong.
camada3: To reflect: System 2 is not always a neutral judge; it is often a lawyer hired by System 1. Who does your reasoning work for when you really want something to be true?
seguir: Cognitive bias: the code of the Matrix.

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Intellectual humility and active open-mindedness
resposta: Intellectual humility is recognizing that your beliefs may be wrong. In 2017, Mark Leary and colleagues at Duke University showed that people with higher intellectual humility paid more attention to the strength of their arguments, judged others less for their religious views, and didn't see a politician changing his mind as a weakness.
aprofundar: Psychologist Jonathan Baron calls actively open thinking the habit of seeking evidence against what you think and weighing that evidence fairly. In the Good Judgment Project forecasting tournament, the best forecasters, called super forecasters, scored higher on this way of thinking. Intellectual humility is not to be without convictions, nor to think that every opinion is worth the same: it is to hold convictions with an open hand. It fits with sincere faith, which need not be afraid to ask questions. The limits: most of these measures come from self-reported questionnaires, and those who call themselves humble are not always humble. Practice: Once a week, look for the best argument against one of your beliefs from someone you respect, and summarize that argument in a way that the author himself would approve.
camada3: To contemplate: in many traditions, the teacher is the one who remains the disciple. When was the last time you changed your mind about something important, and you were thankful for it?
seguir: Calibration: certainty, accuracy and the Dunning-Kruger effect

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Epistemic vigilance: whom to trust
resposta: No one can check everything by himself; we live by trusting others. In 2010, anthropologist Dan Sperber and colleagues called epistemic surveillance the set of defenses we use to avoid being deceived: we evaluate who's speaking, whether they're competent, whether they're interested, and whether what they're saying matches what we already know.
aprofundar: It shows up early: Three- and four-year-olds already prefer to learn from the one who got it right before the one who got it wrong. Cognitive scientist Hugo Mercier, in his 2020 book Not Born Yesterday, argues that we are less gullible than we think; the greatest danger is when surveillance is intentionally turned off, such as when we are taught that asking is rebellion or lack of faith. Three questions are helpful before any authority, religious, political or scientific: Does she really know this? What's in it for her if I believe her? Does what she says match up with other independent sources? To depart from dogma is not to despise anyone's faith: it is to exchange blind obedience for open-eyed trust. The hypothesis part -- how much of this surveillance is innate and how much is learned -- is still up for debate. Practice: Pick one statement you heard from an authority this week, and answer the three questions in writing.
camada3: "But who do you say I am? " he asked his disciples. The question doesn't offend the truth. What question did you stop asking out of fear?
seguir: Getting out of the Matrix in practice

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Lucid dreaming and metacognition: the same light on?
palavras: lucid dreaming and metacognition the same light on
resposta: Lucid dreaming is knowing you're dreaming without waking up, and that's an act of metacognition: the mind perceives its own state. In 2015, Elisa Filevich and colleagues at the Max Planck Institute in Berlin found that people who have lucid dreams frequently have more gray matter in the frontal cortex, a region that also activates when we monitor our own waking thoughts.
aprofundar: In the same study, this region became more active in lucid dreamers during a task of monitoring one's thoughts. It was already known that in ordinary dreams, the frontal lobes of the brain become less active, which helps explain why we accept absurdities without being surprised. In 2014, Ursula Voss and colleagues reported that a weak electric current applied to the head during REM sleep, at rhythms of twenty-five and forty times per second, increased self-awareness in dreams. The caveat: the studies are small, the 2015 comparison is a correlation, and the 2014 result still needs to be replicated by other groups. So the bottom line: the link between metacognition and lucidity is hypothesized; that lucid dreaming exists is proven. Practice: several times a day, ask yourself honestly: Am I dreaming? Read a text twice and look at your hands. The habit of questioning one's state may appear in the dream.
camada3: To contemplate: traditions say that waking life is also a kind of dream. If the same question wakes you in the dream, what would it do if you took it seriously now: am I awake?
seguir: Measure metacognition: the meta-d line and the prefrontal cortex

grupo: Despertar da Matrix e Expansão de Consciência
tema: Witness and meta-consciousness: tradition and science
palavras: witness and meta-consciousness tradition and science
resposta: Contemplative traditions speak of a witness: the consciousness that sees thoughts without being swept away by them. In the Vedanta, it's called sakshi. Science can't confirm an eternal witness, but it studies something nearby and measurable: meta-consciousness, the moment you realize where your attention has gone.
aprofundar: Psychologist Jonathan Schooler has shown that the mind wanders in two ways: when you know you're distracted, and when it wanders without realizing it, like reading a whole page without remembering anything. It's the second way, without meta-consciousness, that gets you the most wrong. In 2015, Cortland Dahl, Antoine Lutz, and Richard Davidson proposed dividing meditations into three families: those of attention, those that build qualities like compassion, and those that deconstruct the idea of a fixed self, by insight. Meta-consciousness is trained in all of them. Honest seals: testimony as ultimate reality is tradition; meta-consciousness as skill is science in the making, with measures still imperfect, because it depends on one's own account. Practice: set a low alarm to ring three times a day; when it rings, respond without judgment: where was my attention, and did I know that?
camada3: To contemplate: the Zen master Dōgen wrote: to study the path is to study the self; to study the self is to forget the self. When you observe the mind, what is left when the observer himself becomes still?
seguir: Default mode network: the inner chatterbox

tema: Advanced protocol: metacognitive diary and the mirror question
palavras: advanced protocol metacognitive diary and the mirror question
resposta: This is a 10-minute daily workout that combines what the previous lessons showed. At night, write down a time during the day when you felt certain, felt strongly, or decided something. Then ask the mirror question: If I believed otherwise, what evidence would I be looking for, and what would I be seeing now?
aprofundar: The protocol has five steps. One: the fact, without interpretation. Two: automatic thought, in quotes. Three: your certainty, from zero to a hundred, to practice calibration. Four: the mirror question, to train the open mind. Five: a rule for tomorrow, like if it happens again, then I'll do such a thing. The basis: A 2006 meta-analysis by Joanne Frattaroli of 146 studies found a small but real effect of writing about one's own experience; and studies on reflective practice suggest that thinking about what you've done in writing improves learning. Honesty: each piece has some support, but this protocol, as a package, was assembled here on the Portal and has not been tested in research; treat it as a personal experiment. It's no substitute for therapy when the pain is great. Practice: Do it for thirty days, and at the end, read it all over again. Look for patterns: what certainties were wrong, and what fears were not fulfilled.
camada3: To contemplate: the mirror does not argue with you; it just shows. The mirror question also does not make you change your mind; it only asks if you have the courage to look. What would you see today?
seguir: Calibration: certainty, accuracy and the Dunning-Kruger effect
